title: Design Twitter for Millions of Users
description: A microblogging platform at Twitter/X scale — tweet ingestion, hybrid fan-out timelines, typeahead search, and real-time notifications, each broken into its own diagram.
summary:
### 1. Tweet Ingestion & Write Path

Handles the moment a tweet is created: validating content, minting a globally unique ID, persisting the tweet, and kicking off everything that has to happen next.

- A dedicated ID Generation Service mints Snowflake-style IDs so tweet IDs are unique and roughly time-sortable without a single central counter
- Media uploads bypass the API tier entirely via pre-signed URLs straight to object storage
- Every write ends with a single Kafka event — the write path never blocks on fan-out, search indexing, or notifications

### 2. Home Timeline Generation (Read Path)

Serves the personalized feed a user sees on open, in well under a second.

- A Fan-out Worker continuously drains the tweet-created stream and pushes new tweet IDs onto every follower's precomputed timeline — the classic fan-out-on-write
- Accounts with tens of millions of followers are exempted from push fan-out; their tweets are merged in at read time from a dedicated cache instead
- Redis holds the hot, precomputed timeline; Cassandra is the durable system of record behind it

### 3. Typeahead Search & Full-Text Search

Turns every keystroke in the search box into an instant, ranked suggestion, and serves full-text search over tweets and accounts.

- Suggestions are never ranked on the fly — a sharded, in-memory trie stores each prefix's top-K completions pre-sorted, so a keystroke is a lookup, not a computation
- An offline pipeline aggregates query and click frequency from a log of every search, then periodically rebuilds the trie and atomically swaps it onto the serving shards
- A Redis cache absorbs repeat lookups for hot prefixes before they ever reach a trie shard

### 4. Notifications & Trending Topics

Fans engagement events (likes, retweets, replies, mentions) out to the people who need to see them, and surfaces what's trending right now.

- Engagement events flow through a shared Kafka topic, decoupling the action that caused a notification from however many notifications it produces
- A Notification Worker writes to a per-user notification feed and forwards eligible events to a push gateway for delivery even when the app is closed
- A separate Trending Aggregator keeps a sliding-window count of hashtag/topic volume in Redis, refreshed independently of the notification path

nodes.name: Client (Mobile/Web)
nodes.details: The origin of every tweet — mobile app or web client. It debounces nothing here (unlike the search box); a post is a single deliberate submit, not a per-keystroke stream.

nodes.name: API Gateway
nodes.details: Terminates TLS, authenticates the user, and rate-limits post volume per account before anything reaches the Tweet Service.

nodes.name: Tweet Service
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Validates tweet length and content
- Requests a unique ID from the ID Generation Service
- Writes the tweet row and publishes the 'tweet_created' event

This service never touches media bytes or follower lists directly — both are delegated so it stays fast under sustained write load.

failure.userImpact: Tweeting fails — users cannot post new content. But timelines, search, and notifications keep working from cached data.

blastRadius.note: health checks fail; no healthy upstream to route to
no new events to publish — fan-out pipeline idles

failure.mitigation: The service is **stateless behind the gateway** — health checks eject bad instances and autoscaling replaces them. The write path is the only casualty; the read path (timelines, search) is fully independent.

nodes.name: ID Generation Service
nodes.details: Mints 64-bit IDs from a timestamp + worker ID + sequence number, so every tweet ID is globally unique and roughly time-sortable without a shared counter or a database round trip.

nodes.name: Media Storage (S3)
nodes.details: Receives media uploads directly from the client via a pre-signed URL. Video/image bytes never pass through the API tier, which only ever handles small JSON payloads.

nodes.name: Tweet Store (Cassandra)
nodes.details: The system of record for tweet content, partitioned by tweet ID for even write distribution. Optimized for high-throughput sequential writes and point reads by ID.

failure.userImpact: New tweets cannot be persisted — tweeting fails. Existing tweets remain readable from the cache and CDN. Timeline hydration for old tweets is lost.

blastRadius.note: can neither write new tweets nor hydrate existing ones at read time
the same Cassandra cluster serves both write and timeline paths

failure.mitigation: Cassandra's **replication factor and cross-region replicas** tolerate node loss as routine. The Redis timeline cache keeps precomputed feeds serving even if the backing store is briefly offline.

nodes.name: Social Graph Store
nodes.details: A dedicated adjacency store for the follow graph, isolated from tweet content so it can be sharded and scaled purely by lookup pattern — 'who follows this account' is on the hot path for every single fan-out.

nodes.name: Tweet Events (Kafka)
nodes.details: Every successful tweet write ends with one event here. Everything downstream — timeline fan-out, search indexing, notifications — consumes from this topic independently, so the write path never blocks on any of them.

failure.userImpact: Tweeting itself still works — the Tweet Service writes to Cassandra first. But timelines freeze, search indexing stops, and notifications halt until Kafka recovers.

blastRadius.note: no events to consume — fan-out pipeline stalls
drains backlog once available but goes idle during outage

failure.mitigation: Kafka is replicated and survives broker failures. Producers buffer events in-memory during brief outages; a reconciliation job can re-enqueue missed events by scanning tweet creation timestamps.

nodes.name: Fan-out Dispatcher
nodes.details: Consumes 'tweet_created' events and reads the author's follower count from the Social Graph Store. Below the celebrity threshold it triggers push fan-out (see diagram 2); above it, the tweet is left for pull-based fan-in at read time.

failure.userImpact: Users notice nothing immediately — tweets still persist. But the fan-out pipeline stalls: non-celebrity tweets never reach followers' timelines until the dispatcher recovers.

blastRadius.note: no events forwarded — no timeline updates to process
events accumulate; offset lag grows

failure.mitigation: The dispatcher is **stateless** — it can restart and resume from its last Kafka offset. A reconciliation worker periodically scans recent tweets and re-dispatches any that were never fanned out.

nodes.name: Client (Mobile/Web)
nodes.details: Requests the home timeline on app open and on pull-to-refresh.

nodes.name: API Gateway
nodes.details: Authenticates the timeline request and routes it to the Timeline Service.

nodes.name: Timeline Service
nodes.details: Reads the precomputed tweet-ID list from Redis, hydrates full tweet content from the Tweet Store, and merges in any pull-model (celebrity) tweets before returning the feed — the whole call is budgeted for well under a second.

nodes.name: Fan-out Worker
nodes.details: Continuously drains the tweet-created stream for non-celebrity authors, reads their follower list, and writes the new tweet ID onto every follower's timeline — both the durable store and the hot cache.

nodes.name: Timeline Store (Cassandra)
nodes.details: Partitioned by user ID, clustered by tweet time. The durable record of each user's fanned-out timeline, rebuilt into Redis on a cache miss.

failure.userImpact: Timeline reads for users not in the Redis cache fail — cold starts, dormant users returning, and cache evictions all turn into errors. Already cached feeds keep working.

blastRadius.note: cache miss → fallback to database fails; nothing to warm from
cache-only mode; only users with warm caches get feeds

failure.mitigation: Cassandra replication tolerates node loss. The Fan-out Worker continues writing to surviving replicas, and once recovered, the cache re-warms naturally through read-backfill.

nodes.name: Timeline Cache (Redis)
nodes.details: Holds the top ~800 precomputed tweet IDs per active user. This is the fast path — most timeline reads never touch Cassandra at all.

failure.userImpact: Timeline reads slow down dramatically but don't break — every request now falls through to the durable Timeline Store (Cassandra). Page load times jump from ~3ms to ~15ms.

blastRadius.note: takes 100× its usual read traffic; hot partitions may saturate
response times climb with every slow database read

failure.mitigation: Redis here is a **read-through cache**, never the source of truth — losing it costs latency, not data. Cassandra keeps serving and re-warms the cache key by key as reads back-fill it.

nodes.name: Social Graph Store
nodes.details: The same follow-graph store used by the Fan-out Dispatcher in diagram 1, duplicated here since diagrams don't share edges — the Fan-out Worker reads it to know who to push to.

nodes.name: Tweet Store (Cassandra)
nodes.details: The same tweet content store from diagram 1, duplicated here — the Timeline Service hydrates full tweet bodies from it after resolving the ID list.

nodes.name: Celebrity Tweet Cache
nodes.details: Caches the most recent tweets from high-follower accounts that are exempt from push fan-out, so merging them into a requester's timeline at read time is a cache hit, not a cold query.

nodes.name: Client (Mobile/Web)
nodes.details: Debounces keystrokes client-side before sending a prefix request — cutting requests for a word like 'car' from three to roughly one.

nodes.name: API Gateway
nodes.details: Routes keystroke-level typeahead requests and full search submissions to their respective services.

nodes.name: Typeahead Service
nodes.details: Serves ranked completions for a partial query. Checks Redis first, falls back to the trie shard cluster, and asynchronously logs every query for the offline ranking pipeline.

failure.userImpact: Typeahead suggestions stop working entirely — users see no autocomplete dropdown. Full-text search (an independent service) is unaffected.

blastRadius.note: prefix routes return errors; search routes still work
no queries to log — offline pipeline idles
no lookups reaching it — cache entries expire unused

failure.mitigation: The Typeahead Service is **stateless** and can restart under the gateway's health check. The Redis cache survives the outage and will warm back up as requests resume.

nodes.name: Search Service
nodes.details: Handles a submitted search query end-to-end, querying the Elasticsearch index for matching tweets and accounts. This is a separate, heavier path from typeahead's per-keystroke lookups.

nodes.name: Suggestion Cache (Redis)
nodes.details: Absorbs repeat requests for the same hot prefixes so they never spend trie-shard CPU at all — even an O(prefix length) memory lookup costs something at 500K requests/sec.

nodes.name: Trie Shard Cluster
nodes.details:
### Design

- Each node caches its top-K completions pre-sorted by popularity — a keystroke is a lookup, not a ranking computation
- Radix compression collapses single-child chains to shrink memory footprint
- Busy prefixes are split across more shards than rare ones (skew-aware sharding)

The whole ranked trie is small enough (single-digit GB) to live fully in memory across the shard fleet.

failure.userImpact: Typeahead degrades noticeably — the Redis cache still serves hot prefixes from its 5-minute TTL, but any miss that would fall through to the trie fails. After the cache drains, all suggestions disappear.

blastRadius.note: entries expire with nowhere to refill from; cold prefix lookups fail
every prefix miss becomes an error; only cached hits survive

failure.mitigation: Trie shards are **replicated and sharded** — losing one node only drops a fraction of prefixes. The Trie Builder can quickly re-deploy a fresh trie to replacement shards, and the Redis cache bridges the gap with warm prefixes.

nodes.name: Search Index (Elasticsearch)
nodes.details: Inverted index over tweet text, hashtags, and account bios, powering the full search path (as opposed to prefix typeahead, which never touches this index).

nodes.name: Query Log (Kafka)
nodes.details: Every typeahead request (and, where available, the suggestion the user clicked) is logged here asynchronously — the raw material the offline ranking pipeline aggregates from.

nodes.name: Aggregation Job
nodes.details: Consumes the query log and tallies how often each phrase was searched or clicked, filtering out low-frequency noise before it ever influences ranking.

nodes.name: Query Frequency Store
nodes.details: Holds rolled-up query popularity counts. Entries older than the retention window are dropped so the trie stays sized to genuinely current query patterns, not historical noise.

nodes.name: Trie Builder
nodes.details: On a fixed cadence (minutes to hours, not real time), reads the latest frequency data and builds a fresh ranked trie from scratch, then atomically swaps it onto the serving shards — the hot read path never pays a rebuild cost.

nodes.name: Client (Mobile/Web)
nodes.details: Displays the notification feed and trending-topics module, and is the eventual target of push delivery.

nodes.name: API Gateway
nodes.details: Routes notification-feed and trending-topic reads to the Notification & Trends Service.

nodes.name: Notification & Trends Service
nodes.details: A read-only API over the Notification Store and Trending Cache — it never computes anything itself, just serves what the async workers have already produced.

nodes.name: Engagement Events (Kafka)
nodes.details: The shared event stream for every engagement action. Decouples the action that caused a notification from however many downstream notifications and trend updates it produces.

nodes.name: Notification Worker
nodes.details: Consumes engagement events, builds a notification payload per recipient, appends it to their entry in the Notification Store, and forwards eligible events to the Push Gateway for immediate delivery.

failure.userImpact: Notifications stop arriving entirely — no in-app feed updates and no push notifications. The engagement actions (likes, retweets) themselves succeed without issue.

blastRadius.note: events accumulate; consumer lag grows unbounded
no new writes; reads still serve stale data
no events forwarded for mobile delivery

failure.mitigation: The worker is **stateless** — it resumes from its last Kafka offset on restart. Kafka buffers engagement events during the outage, so no notifications are lost, only delayed.

nodes.name: Notification Store (DynamoDB)
nodes.description: Per-user feed, sharded by user ID
nodes.details: Notification reads are always single-item lookups by user ID, which is exactly DynamoDB's partition-key access pattern — predictable latency even during a viral-tweet write spike.

failure.userImpact: The notification feed in the app goes blank — users see no historical notifications. Push notifications that were already delivered remain on the device, and new likes/retweets still complete.

blastRadius.note: feed queries fail; trending topics still serve from Redis
writes fail; events stay queued in Kafka

failure.mitigation: DynamoDB is a **managed, replicated store** — individual partition failures are rare. Writes buffer in Kafka during the outage and drain on recovery, so no notifications are permanently lost.

nodes.name: Push Gateway (APNs/FCM)
nodes.details: Delivers the notification directly to the recipient's device via Apple/Google push services, working even when the app is closed.

nodes.name: Trending Aggregator
nodes.details: Maintains a sliding-window count of hashtag and topic mentions from the same engagement stream, independent of the per-user notification path, and refreshes the Trending Cache on a short interval.

nodes.name: Trending Cache (Redis)
nodes.details: Holds the current top trending topics, typically partitioned by region, refreshed every few minutes by the Trending Aggregator.

functional: Users can post tweets (with optional images, video, or GIFs), and each tweet appears in followers' timelines within seconds.
Users can follow/unfollow accounts and view a home timeline aggregating tweets from everyone they follow.
Users get instant, ranked suggestions as they type in the search box, and can run full-text search over tweets and accounts.
Users receive near-real-time notifications for likes, retweets, replies, and mentions, even when the app is closed.
The system surfaces trending topics and hashtags computed from recent tweet volume.
nonFunctional: Massive scale — hundreds of millions of daily active users and a firehose of hundreds of millions of tweets per day.
Low latency — the home timeline and search suggestions must both return in well under a second.
High availability — the posting and timeline paths must survive individual node or shard failures with no single point of failure.
Eventual consistency is acceptable almost everywhere (timelines, counts, trends) in exchange for availability and throughput.
Extreme fan-out — a single tweet from a top account must reach tens of millions of followers within seconds.

stages.title: The MVP — tweet ingestion only
stages.narrative:
The simplest version of the system: a client submits a tweet through an API gateway to a Tweet Service, which mints a globally unique ID via a Snowflake-style generator, persists the tweet in Cassandra, and issues pre-signed URLs so media uploads bypass the API tier entirely.

There are **no timelines, no search, no notifications** — just the core write path. Every tweet is written synchronously, and users read by scanning the database directly. This works for a few thousand users but collapses under millions.

stages.title: Add precomputed timelines — fan-out-on-write
stages.trigger: With millions of users, scanning every tweet to find those from followed accounts is thousands of times too slow — we need precomputed feeds
stages.narrative:
A Kafka event bus decouples the write path from the read path. After persisting a tweet, the Tweet Service publishes a **tweet_created** event. A Fan-out Dispatcher reads the author's follower count from the Social Graph Store and decides between push (most users) and pull (celebrities with 50M+ followers).

The Fan-out Worker continuously drains the stream and pushes tweet IDs onto every follower's precomputed timeline in both the durable Cassandra store and the Redis cache. The Timeline Service now assembles feeds by reading precomputed ID lists from Redis, hydrating full tweet content from the Tweet Store, and merging in celebrity tweets from a dedicated pull cache — all in well under a second.

stages.title: Add notifications and trending topics
stages.trigger: With engagement growing, users need real-time alerts when their content is liked or mentioned, and the platform must surface what is trending right now
stages.narrative:
Engagement events — likes, retweets, replies, mentions — flow through a shared Kafka topic decoupled from the action that caused them. A Notification Worker consumes each event, builds a per-recipient payload, appends it to a DynamoDB Notification Store sharded by user ID, and forwards eligible events to the Push Gateway (APNs/FCM) for immediate mobile delivery.

Independently, the Trending Aggregator maintains a sliding-window count of hashtag and topic mentions from the same engagement stream, refreshing a Redis cache with the top-N topics per region. The Notification & Trends Service serves both feeds as a read-only API — it never computes anything itself.

stages.title: Add typeahead search and full-text search
stages.trigger: At hundreds of millions of users, users expect instant, ranked suggestions with every keystroke and full-text search across tweets and accounts — browsing timelines is no longer enough
stages.narrative:
A Typeahead Service serves prefix suggestions by checking Redis first (hot prefix cache), then falling back to a sharded cluster of in-memory ranked tries where every node stores its top-K completions pre-sorted by popularity — **a keystroke is a lookup, not a computation**.

Offline, a Query Log in Kafka feeds an Aggregation Job that tallies query frequencies. The Trie Builder periodically reads fresh frequencies and atomically swaps a newly built trie onto the serving shards, so the hot read path never pays a rebuild cost. Separately, the Search Service handles full-text queries over the Elasticsearch index for submitted searches — a heavier path than typeahead's per-keystroke lookups.

This is the finished architecture: four semi-independent sub-systems — write path, timeline, notifications, search — each decoupled by Kafka, each scaling on its own signal.

flows.title: Post a tweet
flows.description: The write path — from compose to a durable, event-published tweet. Scoped entirely to frame 1.

steps.text: The client sends the tweet through the API Gateway to the Tweet Service, which requests a globally unique, time-sortable ID from the ID Generation Service before persisting anything.

payload.title: POST /api/tweet

stateChanges.note: Snowflake ID minted — timestamp + worker + sequence

steps.text: If the tweet has an attached image or video, the client uploads the media directly to blob storage using a pre-signed URL issued by the Tweet Service — the media bytes never pass through the API tier.

payload.title: PUT {presigned-url}
payload.body:
Content-Length: 2097152
Content-Type: image/jpeg

‹ 2 MB of image bytes ›

stateChanges.note: media object stored; referenced by tweet metadata

steps.text: The Tweet Service writes the tweet to the sharded Cassandra store, then publishes a 'tweet_created' event to Kafka so downstream systems can react without blocking the write.

The Fan-out Dispatcher consumes the event and reads the author's follower list from the Social Graph Store to decide, based on follower count, whether to push or leave the tweet for pull-based fan-in.

stateChanges.note: follower count read; celebrity threshold exceeded → pull strategy

flows.title: Load the home timeline
flows.description: The read path — how a user's feed is assembled with sub-second latency. Scoped entirely to frame 2.

steps.text: The client requests the home timeline through the API Gateway; the Timeline Service reads the precomputed list of tweet IDs from the Redis cache — the fast path built ahead of time by fan-out-on-write.

payload.title: GET /api/home_timeline
payload.body:
→ Redis LRANGE user:12345:tweets 0 200
→ 200 tweet IDs served from memory in ~3ms

stateChanges.note: cache hit — 200 precomputed tweet IDs returned in ~3ms

steps.text: Full tweet content is hydrated from the Tweet Store, and tweets from celebrity accounts — which use pull-based fan-out to avoid a write explosion — are merged in from a dedicated cache at read time.

payload.title: Hydrate + merge celebrity tweets
payload.body:
→ SELECT * FROM tweets WHERE tweetId IN (...)
→ Redis ZREVRANGE celeb:user:12345:tweets 0 20

stateChanges.note: celebrity tweets merged into feed at read time

steps.text: Independently of any single read, the Fan-out Worker is continuously draining the tweet-created event stream: for each new tweet it reads the author's follower list and pushes the tweet ID onto every follower's durable timeline.

stateChanges.note: tweet ID appended to each follower's timeline row

steps.text: The worker also writes the same tweet ID into the Redis timeline cache, so the next time any of those followers opens the app, their feed is already sitting in memory.

stateChanges.note: tweet ID pushed onto each follower's hot timeline cache

flows.title: Type-ahead search suggestions
flows.description: How a keystroke becomes an instant, ranked suggestion. Scoped entirely to frame 3.

steps.text: As the user types each character, the client — after debouncing keystrokes to cut request volume by roughly two-thirds — sends the current prefix through the API Gateway to the Typeahead Service.

The Typeahead Service checks the Redis suggestion cache first. On a hit it returns instantly; on a miss, it queries the sharded trie cluster, where suggestions for that prefix were already ranked and sorted ahead of time.

payload.title: Redis GET prefix:dece
payload.body:
→ MISS (or HIT: ["decentralized", "december", "decency"])
→ Trie shard lookup: prefix='dece' → O(k) trie traversal

stateChanges.note: cache miss; falling back to trie shard cluster

steps.text: The trie shard's answer is written back into the Redis cache, so the next request for the same prefix — extremely likely given how skewed real query traffic is — never has to touch the trie at all.

stateChanges.note: trie result cached — next identical prefix is a Redis hit

steps.text: Every prefix query is also logged asynchronously onto a Kafka topic, feeding the offline pipeline that keeps the trie's popularity rankings current.

stateChanges.note: query logged asynchronously for offline aggregation

flows.title: Rebuild the suggestion trie offline
flows.description: The offline pipeline that keeps typeahead rankings fresh without ever blocking a live query. Scoped entirely to frame 3.

steps.text: An Aggregation Job continuously consumes the raw query log from Kafka and tallies how often each search phrase was typed and clicked.
Counts are rolled up into the Query Frequency Store, with low-frequency phrases filtered out and entries past the retention window discarded to bound the trie's size.
On a fixed cadence — minutes to hours, not real time — the Trie Builder reads the latest frequencies and constructs an entirely fresh, ranked trie in the background.

payload.title: Build trie from frequencies
payload.body:
Read 10M prefix counts
→ Build radix tree
→ Sort top-K completions per node

steps.text: The new trie is atomically swapped onto the serving shards, so live query latency never pays a rebuild cost — the system trades a little staleness for a lookup that's always fast.

payload.title: Atomic swap → new trie live
payload.body:
shard-1: swap(/data/trie/v2 → /data/trie/current)
shard-2: swap(/data/trie/v2 → /data/trie/current)
shard-N: swap(/data/trie/v2 → /data/trie/current)

stateChanges.note: fresh ranked trie swapped in — lookups now reflect latest query frequencies

flows.title: Deliver a notification
flows.description: From an engagement action to a push notification and a readable feed. Scoped entirely to frame 4.

steps.text: A like, retweet, reply, or mention is published as an event onto the shared Engagement Events topic, decoupling the action from however many notifications it fans out into.

stateChanges.note: engagement event published — Notification Worker consumes asynchronously

steps.text: The Notification Worker consumes the event, builds the notification payload, and appends it to the recipient's entry in the Notification Store, sharded by user ID.

stateChanges.note: notification appended to recipient's feed; sharded by userId

steps.text: The same event is forwarded to a Push Gateway (APNs/FCM), which delivers it straight to the recipient's device even if the app is closed.

stateChanges.note: push notification delivered to device via APNs/FCM

steps.text: When the user later opens the app, the Notification & Trends Service reads their notification feed and the current trending topics directly from storage and cache — no recomputation needed.

payload.title: GET /api/notifications + GET /api/trending
payload.body:
→ DynamoDB Query(userId = @elonmusk, limit 50)
→ Redis ZREVRANGE trending:global 0 10

stateChanges.note: trending topics served from Redis — no recomputation at read time

decisions.title: Tweet ID generation
decisions.rationale: At ~6,000 writes/sec sustained (and much higher during spikes), a single auto-increment counter becomes a contention point, and per-shard counters can collide across shards. A Snowflake-style generator produces IDs from a timestamp, worker ID, and sequence number, giving global uniqueness and rough time-ordering with zero coordination between nodes.

decisions.title: Timeline: hybrid fan-out
decisions.choice: Push (fan-out-on-write) for most users, pull (fan-out-on-read) for celebrities
decisions.rationale: An account with 50M+ followers would require 50M+ timeline writes per tweet under pure push — the estimates make that write explosion untenable. Pure pull would make every timeline read for every user pay a fan-in join, which is too slow at ~1000:1 read-to-write ratio. The hybrid splits the difference: most users get a precomputed, instant feed, while the rare high-follower accounts are merged in at read time.

decisions.title: Search: precompute rankings, don't compute them per query
decisions.choice: Trie with top-K suggestions cached at every node
alternatives: Rank candidates live from a query-time index
decisions.rationale: At a peak of 500K suggest requests/sec, ranking candidates on every keystroke is not viable. Precomputing each prefix's top-K completions ahead of time turns every request into a lookup instead of a computation — the core insight behind both referenced typeahead designs.

decisions.title: Search: offline rebuild cadence
decisions.choice: Batch rebuild (minutes to hours) with atomic swap, plus a lightweight real-time overlay
alternatives: Update the trie in place on every query
decisions.rationale: In-place updates to a structure being read 500K times a second would require locking that the hot path can't afford. Rebuilding fresh and swapping atomically keeps every live read lock-free; a small real-time overlay covers the gap for suddenly trending terms without paying for a full rebuild.

decisions.title: Notification storage
alternatives: Relational table joined at read time
decisions.rationale: Notification reads are always single-item lookups by user ID — exactly DynamoDB's partition-key access pattern. This gives predictable latency even during a viral-tweet spike that floods the write path with mentions and likes for one popular thread.

decisions.title: Social graph storage
decisions.choice: Dedicated adjacency store, separate from tweet content
alternatives: Follower lists as rows in the same store as tweets
decisions.rationale: Follower lookups sit on the hot path for every fan-out decision and every timeline push, at a completely different volume and access pattern than tweet writes. Isolating the graph store lets it be sharded and scaled by adjacency-lookup load rather than being coupled to tweet throughput.

bottlenecks.title: Timeline: celebrity write explosion
bottlenecks.problem: A tweet from an account with 50M+ followers would need 50M+ timeline writes within seconds if fanned out naively, overwhelming the Timeline Store and the Fan-out Worker.
bottlenecks.mitigation: The Fan-out Dispatcher routes celebrity tweets away from push fan-out entirely. Their tweets are fetched on demand from the Celebrity Tweet Cache and merged into each requester's timeline at read time instead.

bottlenecks.title: Search: hot prefix skew
bottlenecks.problem: A small number of popular prefixes receive a hugely disproportionate share of the 500K/s suggest traffic, which can overload whichever single trie shard happens to own them.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Skew-aware prefix sharding splits busy prefixes across more shards than rare ones, and the Suggestion Cache absorbs a large fraction of repeat hits before they ever reach a shard.

bottlenecks.title: Search: trending term lag
bottlenecks.problem: With only a periodic offline rebuild (minutes to hours), a breaking-news term can spike in seconds and stay invisible in suggestions until the next rebuild cycle.
bottlenecks.mitigation: A lightweight real-time overlay is blended into typeahead results at query time, and the separate Trending Aggregator keeps its own short sliding window in Redis independent of the trie rebuild cadence.

bottlenecks.title: Notifications: viral tweet thundering herd
bottlenecks.problem: A single viral tweet can generate millions of mention, like, and reply events within minutes, all needing to fan out through the Notification Worker and Push Gateway simultaneously.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Kafka buffers the engagement event burst so the Notification Worker drains it at a sustainable rate rather than being hit synchronously, and notification writes are batched per recipient shard.

bottlenecks.title: Timeline: cold-follower cache stampede
bottlenecks.problem: A user who hasn't opened the app in a while has no warm entry in the Timeline Cache; if many dormant users return around the same event, that's a burst of cold reads hitting the Timeline Store at once.
bottlenecks.mitigation: The durable Timeline Store in Cassandra is sized for this fallback path, and cache repopulation happens lazily on read rather than requiring a full timeline recomputation.

quiz.question: Why does Twitter mint tweet IDs with a dedicated ID Generation Service instead of relying on each database shard's own auto-increment counter?
quiz.answer: A Snowflake-style generator combines a timestamp, worker ID, and sequence number to produce IDs that are globally unique and roughly time-sortable across every shard, with no shared counter to contend on. Per-shard auto-increment would either collide across shards or require coordination that doesn't scale to thousands of writes per second.

quiz.question: An account has 50 million followers. What would go wrong if every tweet from that account triggered fan-out-on-write, and how does this design avoid it?
quiz.answer: Fan-out-on-write would mean 50 million-plus timeline writes within seconds of a single tweet, overwhelming the Fan-out Worker and Timeline Store. The Fan-out Dispatcher instead routes high-follower accounts to a pull model: their tweets sit in a Celebrity Tweet Cache and are merged into each requester's timeline at read time, so the cost is paid once per reader, not once per follower per tweet.

quiz.question: Why does the Typeahead Service check Redis before ever touching a trie shard, when the trie lookup is already just an in-memory read?
quiz.answer: Even an O(prefix length) trie lookup costs CPU at 500K requests/sec, and real query traffic is heavily skewed toward a small set of hot prefixes. Redis absorbs those repeat identical requests entirely, so the trie shards only ever see the long tail of genuinely distinct lookups.

quiz.question: The Trie Builder only rebuilds the whole suggestion trie every few minutes to hours. What's the risk, and what covers the gap?
quiz.answer: A term that suddenly starts trending — breaking news, for example — would be invisible in suggestions until the next scheduled rebuild. This is covered by a lightweight real-time overlay blended into typeahead results at query time, and separately by the Trending Aggregator's own short sliding window that updates the Trending Cache far more frequently than the trie rebuild cycle.

quiz.question: Why does the Social Graph Store appear as a separate node in both the Tweet Ingestion diagram and the Home Timeline diagram, instead of one shared node with an edge drawn between the two diagrams?
quiz.answer: Each diagram in this design is meant to be read independently, so edges never cross between frames. When two diagrams genuinely depend on the same underlying store — here, the follow graph is read by both the Fan-out Dispatcher and the Fan-out Worker — the node is duplicated in each diagram (noted as 'Shared with Write Path') rather than drawing a connection across an otherwise self-contained diagram.

quiz.question: Engagement events (likes, retweets, mentions) could have called the Notification Worker directly. Why route them through Kafka instead?
quiz.answer: Kafka decouples the moment an engagement action happens from however many notifications and trend updates it eventually produces. It buffers bursts — like the millions of interactions a viral tweet generates in minutes — so the Notification Worker and Trending Aggregator can each drain the stream at their own sustainable pace instead of being hit synchronously and falling over.
